stories.blurb: Joseph hands over the Thursday five-a-side to Ruby, and she wants to know exactly what she is signing.

opener.setting: Thursday, 9:20pm. The sports hall car park after five-a-side. Joseph holds a net bag of bibs on one shoulder and the hall key in his fist.

lines.text: “Eleven months I've booked the hall, chased the fee and washed the bibs. I'm handing it over tonight, or I'm only ever playing.”
“Then hand it to me. But I'm not catching it on the move. Say exactly what it is.”
lines.cue: palm out, nothing in it yet

opener.ask: What has to be in a deal before it holds?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: A deal that holds has four things in it. Both sides say yes to the same clear thing. Each side gives something. Both are fit to agree. Nothing in it has to be hidden. Tap the one each line is making sure of.

items.text: “Every Thursday you collect the pitch fee before kick-off and hand it to Mr Pell by Friday. Can you say yes to that?”
items.why: He has named the exact job, the day and the hand-over, and asked for a yes to it. Next week, both of them can say what was agreed.

traps.0: Above board. Nothing is hidden, but the line asks Ruby to accept a set job. Whether the job is allowed is a separate question.
traps.2: Something each way. It sounds like a swap, but only Ruby's side is named here, so nothing goes back to her yet.

items.example:
Allotment association, Saturday.
Chair: “You hold the gate key and lock up by dusk. Do you agree?”
You: “Agreed. Dusk.”
Chair: “Noted.”

items.text: “If I take the booking, the bibs and the cones, what do you do? I'm not volunteering for the whole of Thursday.”
items.cue: arms folded, bib hanging off her wrist
items.why: She is asking what comes back to her. A deal needs something going each way, or one person gives and the other takes.

traps.0: Fit to agree. It sounds like she is testing his state of mind, but the line says nothing about whether he can follow the deal.
traps.1: A clear yes. She will want one in the end, but this line asks what she gets, not whether she agrees to a set job.

items.example:
Book club, last Tuesday.
Host: “I'll pick the books if you do the venue.”
You: “Fine, and I'll bring the wine.”
Host: “Then it's even.”

items.text: “My nephew Callum is fourteen and wants a game. His mum signs the form first. He can say yes all he likes.”
items.cue: flicking the form against her palm
items.why: Callum can't agree to a deal on his own at fourteen, so the adult who answers for him joins in. She is checking who is fit to say yes.

traps.1: Above board. Nothing here breaks a rule. The worry is whether a fourteen-year-old can agree alone.
traps.2: A clear yes. He may well give one, but the line is about whether his yes counts by itself.

items.example:
Swimming club, Saturday.
Coach: “Your daughter's eleven, so a parent signs the trip form.”
Parent: “Of course.”
Coach: “Then she can come.”

items.text: “Mr Pell says the slot is ours to play in, not to rent out. We don't pass it to the netball lot for cash.”
items.cue: pointing his key at the hall doors
items.why: He is keeping the deal inside the hall's rules. A deal that holds has nothing in it that has to be hidden from the caretaker.

traps.0: Something each way. A rent-out would be a swap, but this line is about whether the swap is allowed at all.
traps.1: Fit to agree. Nobody's state of mind is in question here, only whether the plan breaks the hall's rule.

items.example:
Car park, Sunday.
Neighbour: “I'll rent your drive for the match on Saturday.”
You: “The council lets only residents park there. I can't.”
Neighbour: “Fair enough.”

rounds.intro: Two sorts. First, build the deal: put each line under the part it covers. Then sort drafts that don't hold.

items.prompt: Build the deal. Tap a line, then the part of the deal it covers.

items.text: “From this Thursday you collect the fee at the door and hand it to Mr Pell by Friday. Yes or no?”
items.why: It names the job, the day and the hand-over, and asks for a yes, so both of them can say later what was agreed.

items.text: “Done means the bibs are washed, dry and in the kit bag by the hall door.”
items.why: It says what finished looks like in terms anyone can see from the car park. Steiner wants the aim stated as something you can watch.

items.text: “You run the fee and the cones. I'll book the hall and wash the bibs.”
items.why: Each person gives something and each share is named, so nobody wonders whose Thursday it is.

items.text: “I'll bring the oranges for half-time, and you bring the first-aid kit.”
items.why: One hand brings food and the other brings safety, so neither of them ends up giving more than they get.

items.text: “Callum is fourteen, so his mum is part of this deal too.”
items.why: A young person can't agree on his own, so the adult who answers for him joins in.

items.text: “The slot stays ours. If we ever pass it on, Mr Pell hears first.”
items.why: Nothing in the line has to be hidden from the hall. A deal that holds stays inside the rules.

items.prompt: These drafts don't hold. Put each one under what is wrong with it.

items.text: “Just keep an eye on things, and we'll see how it goes.”
items.why: An eye has no edge. Neither of them could say afterwards what was agreed, and Steiner says vague aims can't be contracted.

items.text: “I'll sub you the fee this week, and you'll know it when I need a lift.”
items.why: The price, a lift later, is never stated as a term. Ruby can't say yes to something she hasn't been told.

items.text: “I'll run the whole rota myself all season. You don't have to do a thing for it.”
items.why: A gift is fine in life. In a deal meant to hold, nothing coming back leaves one giving and the other taking, which is how a rescue starts.

items.text: “It's Ruby's fortieth, she's had four glasses of fizz, and she said yes to the whole rota. Done.”
items.why: A yes from someone in that state doesn't count. The deal waits until she can mean it.

items.text: “We tell Mr Pell we're six and play with twelve at the cheaper rate.”
items.why: The deal depends on hiding something from the hall. Steiner requires an aim that is lawful.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Now the book's words for the four. Steiner's names for them are mutual consent, consideration, competency and lawful object.

items.text: “I'll be more committed to Thursdays.”
items.cue: said at the counter, before the tea arrives. Which explanation fits?
options: It fails mutual consent. Nobody could say next week what was agreed, so there is nothing to say yes to. Steiner wants the aim stated as something you can see someone do.
It fails consideration. Ruby offers a change of heart but asks for nothing, so Joseph would be rescuing her from her own promise and getting a pat on the head for it.
It is a fair start. A good intention is enough to begin with, and the details can come later, once the first few Thursdays have gone by and everyone has seen how it goes.
items.why: Mutual consent needs a clear offer and a clear yes, in terms you could watch happen. 'More committed' is the vague kind of aim Steiner says can't be contracted.

traps.1: Consideration is about what comes back. Ruby is offering something, her own effort. The trouble is nobody can tell what it is.
traps.2: A good intention feels like a start. With nothing anyone can see, the first argument will be about what 'committed' meant.

items.example:
Running club, Tuesday, 6:30pm.
Member: “I'll try to be more committed.”
Captain: “Which nights, and from when?”
Member: “Tuesdays and Saturdays, from this week.”
Now there is something to say yes to.

items.text: “I'll cover the booking and the fee every week from now. You needn't do anything for it.”
items.cue: handing over the key anyway. Ruby says: “Deal.” Which explanation fits?
options: Mutual consent is missing. Ruby only said 'Deal', so she hasn't really agreed to anything and Joseph can't hold her to it.
Competency is missing. Joseph is worn out after eleven months, so his offer doesn't count as a proper one and Ruby can ignore it.
Consideration is missing. Nothing comes back from Ruby, so Joseph gives and Ruby takes. Steiner says that without something in return, helping slides into a rescue.
items.why: The terms are clear and Ruby said yes, so consent is there. What is missing is something from Ruby. Without it, Joseph carries on giving and the helping becomes a rescue.

traps.0: 'Deal' to a clear offer is a yes. The terms are exact, so consent is present.
traps.1: Being tired isn't what Steiner means. He means people who can't understand what they are agreeing to, such as someone drunk or a child alone. Joseph understands his own offer.

items.example:
Neighbours, Sunday morning.
Neighbour: “I'll mow your lawn every week. Don't do anything for it.”
You: “Okay, thanks.”
By July you dread the doorbell, and he is sour about a lawn he never gets thanked for.

lines.text: “Your knee, the stairs, Leo's bag. Somebody has to say who does the gate, and it can't be you every day.”
“Three years I've done it and nobody's died.”
